reels.title: The crash that paused

prediction.prompt: Black Thursday, 24 October 1929: share prices plunge soon after trading opens. How far down is the Dow Jones average when trading closes?

frames.text: A crowd outside the New York Stock Exchange in 1929, after the crash.
On Black Thursday, 24 October, prices fell 11 percent soon after trading opened.
frames.say: On Black Thursday, the twenty-fourth of October, prices fell eleven percent soon after trading opened.

frames.text: Leading bankers had Richard Whitney, of the Exchange, bid $205 a share for US Steel, well above the market.

frames.text: The slide stopped. The Dow closed down only about 2 percent.
Over the next Monday and Tuesday, it fell 23 percent. This front page is from the day after.
By July 1932 it stood 89 percent below its 1929 peak, which it did not regain until 1954.

reels.takeaway: Bankers briefly stopped Black Thursday's slide. By July 1932 the Dow stood 89 percent below its 1929 peak.

reels.title: A parade, not a family line

prediction.prompt: A famous 1965 picture shows apes marching, step by step, into a man. What did the book it appeared in say about the marchers?

choices.label: Each one was the ancestor of the next
Some were side branches or dead ends
Nothing about who descended from whom

frames.text: An ape rises, step by step, into a man at a telescope: a spoof of a famous picture.
Rudolph Zallinger drew the original for a 1965 book. Its 15 figures march as if each became the next.
Yet the book's own text called one marcher a likely side branch, and another a dead end.
The artist never meant a single line, its author said. The picture overpowered the words.
Thomas Henry Huxley's 1863 row of ape and human skeletons became an unintended shorthand for evolution, a historian argues.
Critics say the march wrongly makes evolution look like progress.

reels.takeaway: The famous march was never meant as a line of ancestors: its own book called one marcher a likely side branch and another a dead end.

claims.claim: The image is titled Astronomy Evolution 2
claims.quote: Astronomy Evolution 2

claims.claim: The March of Progress has been widely parodied to make images of other kinds of progress
claims.quote: It has been widely parodied and imitated to create images of progress of other kinds.

claims.claim: Rudolph Zallinger drew it for the Early Man volume, published in 1965
claims.quote: It was created for the Early Man volume of the Life Nature Library, published in 1965, and drawn by the artist Rudolph Zallinger.

claims.claim: Its 15 figures are lined up as if marching in a parade, left to right
claims.quote: The 15 human evolutionary forebears are lined up as if they were marching in a parade from left to right.

claims.claim: It looks like one direct line of ancestors, but the original text knew that reading would be wrong
claims.quote: Contrary to appearances and some complaints, the original 1965 text of "The Road to Homo Sapiens" reveals an understanding of the fact that a linear presentation of a sequence of primate species, all in the direct line of human ancestors, would not be a correct interpretation.

claims.claim: The text called the fourth figure a likely side branch of the human family tree
claims.quote: For example, the fourth of Zallinger's figures (Oreopithecus) is said to be "a likely side branch on man's family tree".

claims.claim: The text called the seventh figure an evolutionary dead end
claims.quote: Likewise, the seventh figure (Paranthropus) is said to be "an evolutionary dead end".

claims.claim: F. Clark Howell, the anthropologist who wrote the section, commented on how it was read
claims.quote: With regard to the way the illustration has been interpreted, the anthropologist and author of the section, F. Clark Howell, remarked

claims.claim: The artist did not intend a linear sequence, but viewers read it that way
claims.quote: The artist didn't intend to reduce the evolution of man to a linear sequence, but it was read that way by viewers.

claims.claim: Howell said the graphic overwhelmed the text
claims.quote: The graphic overwhelmed the text.

claims.claim: Huxley's 1863 frontispiece compared ape and human skeletons, and the historian Jennifer Tucker argues its left-to-right sequence became a shorthand for evolution
claims.quote: Thomas Henry Huxley added a frontispiece to his 1863 book Evidence as to Man's Place in Nature comparing the skeletons of apes and humans, but historian Jennifer Tucker argues that its left-to-right progressionist sequence unintentionally became "an iconic and instantly recognizable visual shorthand for evolution".

claims.claim: The image is Huxley's frontispiece showing the skeletons of apes and man
claims.quote: Frontispiece to Huxley 'Evidence as to man's place in Nature'. Illustration showing skeleton's of apes and man

claims.claim: The March of Progress has been criticised as wrongly implying that evolution is progressive
claims.quote: It has also been criticized as "unintentionally and wrongly" implying that "evolution is progressive".

reels.title: Two real moons and four false ones

prediction.prompt: William Herschel claimed to have seen four extra moons of Uranus in the 1790s. What were they, most likely?

choices.label: Real moons, too faint to see again

frames.text: Uranus and its moons, seen by the James Webb Space Telescope in 2023. Ariel and Umbriel were discovered on 24 October 1851.
frames.say: Uranus and its moons, seen by the James Webb Space Telescope in twenty twenty-three. Ariel and Umbriel were discovered on the twenty-fourth of October, eighteen fifty-one.

frames.text: The British astronomer William Lassell found them both.
Two other moons, Titania and Oberon, had been known since 1787. Their discoverer, William Herschel, claimed four more.
If Herschel had seen extra moons, he should have seen these two. They matched none of his four, which were probably faint stars.
Umbriel, named for a gloomy sprite in a poem by Alexander Pope, is the darkest of Uranus's larger moons.

reels.takeaway: Lassell's two new moons of 1851 showed that William Herschel's four extra moons were probably faint stars.

claims.claim: The image of Uranus and its moons was taken by the James Webb telescope on 4 September 2023

claims.claim: William Lassell discovered Umbriel and Ariel on 24 October 1851
claims.quote: It was discovered on October 24, 1851, by William Lassell at the same time as neighboring moon Ariel.

claims.claim: Herschel claimed four more moons, which were never confirmed
claims.quote: Although William Herschel, the discoverer of Titania and Oberon, claimed at the end of the 18th century that he had observed four additional moons of Uranus, his observations were not confirmed and those four objects are now thought to be spurious.

claims.claim: Herschel believed he saw four more moons in 1790 and 1794
claims.quote: he subsequently believed that he had observed four other moons: two on 18 January and 9 February 1790, and two more on 28 February and 26 March 1794.

claims.claim: Herschel should have seen Ariel and Umbriel if he saw any other moons, and they matched none of his four
claims.quote: Lassell's observations of 1851, in which he discovered Ariel and Umbriel, however, failed to support Herschel's observations; Ariel and Umbriel, which Herschel certainly ought to have seen if he had seen any satellites besides Titania and Oberon, did not correspond to any of Herschel's four additional satellites in orbital characteristics.

claims.claim: Herschel's four moons were probably faint stars mistaken for moons
claims.quote: It was therefore concluded that Herschel's four satellites were spurious, probably arising from the misidentification of faint stars in the vicinity of Uranus as satellites

claims.claim: Umbriel is named for a 'dusky melancholy sprite' in Pope's poem The Rape of the Lock
claims.quote: Umbriel is the "dusky melancholy sprite" in Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock

claims.claim: Umbriel is the darkest of Uranus's larger moons
claims.quote: Umbriel is the darkest of Uranus' larger moons

reels.title: The volcano that was thought extinct

On the evening of 24 October, an ash column rose amid lightning. A ship's captain later put its height by sextant at 27 to 29 kilometres.
frames.say: On the evening of the twenty-fourth of October, an ash column rose amid lightning. A ship's captain later put its height by sextant at twenty-seven to twenty-nine kilometres.

frames.text: The main eruption lasted 18 to 20 hours, among the century's largest. Blasts were heard in Costa Rica, about 850 kilometres away.
It left a new crater, about a kilometre long, seen here full of steam.
The president played it down, with a propaganda fair about to open. The official paper's first report appeared on 3 November.
frames.say: The president played it down, with a propaganda fair about to open. The official paper's first report appeared on the third of November.

reels.takeaway: Santa María had no recorded eruption before 1902. Then its main eruption, one of the 20th century's largest, lasted some 20 hours.

reels.title: Leaves that follow the mother

prediction.prompt: Carl Correns found a plant whose leaf colour comes from its mother, not its father. How did he find out?

choices.label: He crossed each colour both ways, as mother and father
He traced the colour through old seed records
He watched its cells divide under a microscope

frames.text: The German botanist Carl Correns rediscovered Mendel's laws of heredity, publishing in 1900.
Then he took on four o'clock plants with green-and-white leaves, which seemed to defy those laws.
He crossed them both ways. Pollen from a green branch, on a white branch's flower, gave white seedlings.
Pollen from a white branch, on a green branch's flower, gave green ones. Colour followed the mother.
Mendel's traits come from either parent alike. This colour depends on chloroplasts, which here come from the mother alone.
His 1909 paper made it the first conclusive case of inheritance outside the chromosomes.

reels.takeaway: Crossing four o'clocks both ways showed Correns that leaf colour can come from the mother alone.

claims.claim: Correns was a German botanist who discovered the principles of heredity independently of Hugo de Vries
claims.quote: was a German botanist and geneticist notable primarily for his independent discovery of the principles of heredity, which he achieved simultaneously but independently of the botanist Hugo de Vries

claims.claim: He rediscovered and independently verified Mendel's work
claims.quote: He rediscovered and independently verified the work of Mendel in a separate model organism.

claims.claim: He published his first paper on heredity in 1900
claims.quote: Correns published his first paper on 25 January 1900, which cited both Charles Darwin and Mendel, recognising the relevance of genetics to Darwin's ideas.

claims.claim: He experimented with four o'clock plants to investigate apparent exceptions to Mendel's laws in mottled green-and-white leaves
claims.quote: he undertook experiments with the four o'clock plant Mirabilis jalapa to investigate apparent counterexamples to Mendel's laws in the heredity of variegated (green and white mottled) leaf color

claims.claim: Green pollen on a white stigma gave white offspring; white pollen on a green stigma gave green offspring
claims.quote: However, if green pollen fertilized a white stigma, the progeny were white, but if the sexes of the donors were reversed (white pollen on a green stigma), the progeny were green.

claims.claim: Mendelian traits do not depend on which parent passes them on, but leaf colour depended greatly on it
claims.quote: Correns found that, while Mendelian traits behave independently of the sex of the source parent, leaf color depended greatly on which parent had which trait.

claims.claim: Seedlings of a green mother inherit working chloroplasts and so are green
claims.quote: Conversely, if a white father is paired with a green mother with functional chloroplasts, the progeny will only inherit functional chloroplasts, and will thus be green.

claims.claim: In most angiosperms the chloroplasts come only from the mother
claims.quote: since the chloroplasts come exclusively from the mother in most angiosperms

claims.claim: His 1909 paper made variegated leaf colour the first conclusive example of cytoplasmic inheritance
claims.quote: In his 1909 paper, he established variegated leaf color as the first conclusive example of cytoplasmic inheritance.

claims.claim: Cytoplasmic inheritance showed that factors outside the chromosomes shape traits
claims.quote: He also discovered cytoplasmic inheritance, an important extension of Mendel's theories, which demonstrated the existence of extrachromosomal factors on phenotype.

reels.title: The sixty percent mistake

prediction.prompt: Suppose personality traits have a heritability of about 0.6. Which reading of that number is right?

choices.label: 60% of your personality comes from your genes
It is about differences between people, not one person
60 in 100 people inherit their parents' personality

frames.text: Two boys, short and tall, hold corn from a short race and a tall one. Height varies in people and in corn.
Heritability is a statistic about such variation. For personality it has been put as high as 0.6, which is easy to misread as 60 percent of you.
frames.say: Heritability is a statistic about such variation. For personality it has been put as high as zero point six, which is easy to misread as sixty percent of you.

frames.text: That reading is wrong. Heritability measures how much of the variation within a population can be put down to genetic differences.
It does not measure how much of one person's trait comes from their genes.
It holds for one population in one setting. It can shift with no change in genes, if surroundings vary more.

reels.takeaway: Heritability describes the differences within a population. It is not the share of one person's trait that genes caused.

claims.claim: The picture shows a short and a tall boy holding stalks from a short and a tall race of corn
claims.quote: A short and a tall boy each holding a stalk of corn—one stalk of a race of short corn, the other of tall corn.

claims.claim: Heritability estimates how much of the variation in a trait within a population is due to genetic variation
claims.quote: Heritability is a statistic used in the fields of breeding and genetics that estimates the degree of variation in a phenotypic trait in a population that is due to genetic variation between individuals in that population.

claims.claim: Heritability causes confusion because its technical meaning differs from the everyday one
claims.quote: It is the source of much confusion because its technical definition is different from its commonly-understood folk definition.

claims.claim: Even if the heritability of personality is about 0.6, it is incorrect to read that as 60% of your personality being inherited
claims.quote: For example, it is incorrect to say that since the heritability of personality traits is about 0.6, that means that 60% of your personality is inherited from your parents and 40% comes from the environment.

claims.claim: Heritability measures the fraction of variation in a trait that can be attributed to genetic variation
claims.quote: Heritability measures the fraction of phenotype variability that can be attributed to genetic variation.

claims.claim: It is not the fraction of one individual's trait that genes caused
claims.quote: This is not the same as saying that this fraction of an individual phenotype is caused by genetics.

claims.claim: Heritability should not be read as a measure of how far a trait is genetically determined in an individual
claims.quote: The heritability of a trait should not be interpreted as a measure of the extent to which said trait is genetically determined in an individual.

claims.claim: Heritability is specific to one population in one environment
claims.quote: Heritability is specific to a particular population in a particular environment.

claims.claim: Heritability can change with no genetic change, for instance when the environment contributes more variation
claims.quote: In addition, heritability can change without any genetic change occurring, such as when the environment starts contributing to more variation.
